uncited: *   **Input:** Point cloud data (positions, colors) in world space; a projection matrix ($M_{vp}$); image dimensions ($W \times H$).
*   **Data Structure:** A storage buffer acting as a custom framebuffer.
Each pixel corresponds to one 64-bit integer.
*   Bits 0–23 (Lower 24 bits): RGB color (8 bits per channel).
*   Bits 24–55 (Upper 32 bits): Linear depth value (32-bit integer representation of float).
*   **Depth Representation:** Linear depth ($pos.w$) is used directly.
*   **Atomic Operation:** `atomicMin` on 64-bit integers.
Since depth is stored in the upper bits and color in the lower bits, minimizing the integer value effectively selects the point with the smallest depth.

Extract the linear depth from the $w$-component of the clip-space position.
Convert the floating-point depth to an integer representation for packing.
Pack the depth and color into a 64-bit integer.
The color ($rgb$) is assumed to be in the range [0, 1] and converted to 8-bit integers.
Here, $rgb$ is the 24-bit integer formed by $(R \ll 16) \mid (G \ll 8) \mid B$.
**Resolve Pass:** After all points are processed, transfer the results from the storage buffer to an OpenGL texture for display.
Read the packed integer from the framebuffer.
*   **Depth Equality:** If two points have the exact same depth, the `atomicMin` will pick the one with the smaller packed value (i.e., smaller color value).
The method performs early-z testing to discard fragments that are occluded before writing to memory.
It uses warp-level primitives to perform group-wide reduction of points, minimizing global memory contention.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$ for the render pass, where $N$ is the number of points. $O(W \times H)$ for the resolve pass, where $W \times H$ is the image resolution.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(W \times H)$ for the storage buffer (one 64-bit integer per pixel).
*   Avoids the overhead of the standard graphics pipeline.
*   Uses linear depth, avoiding precision loss.
*   Thread-safe and robust for dense point clouds.
*   High performance on modern GPUs with 64-bit atomic support.
*   Requires a storage buffer configured as an interleaved depth and color buffer.
*   May produce holes if point density is insufficient.
*   Requires a resolve pass to transfer data to a displayable texture.

*   **When to use:** When rendering large point clouds on hardware with compute shader support and 64-bit atomic operations, especially when performance is critical and the standard pipeline is too slow or lacks precision.
*   **When not to use:** When the point density is very low and holes are unacceptable without additional hole-filling techniques, or on hardware lacking 64-bit atomic support.
Previous compute-based methods, such as those by Günther et al. [GKLR13], used busy-loops and atomic compare-and-swap, which were less efficient.
Lukac et al. [Lpa14] used a similar `atomicMin`-based algorithm but it was not thread-safe.
Marrs et al. [MWH18] used compute-based rendering for depth reprojection but did not handle colors.
